article.headline: SuperSplat Makes Photorealistic 3D Walkthroughs Free and Browser-Native
article.lede: Three years ago, researchers in France showed that a 3D scene could be encoded as millions of tiny, coloured, semi-transparent ellipsoids and rendered in real time on a consumer graphics chip — a technique that quickly eclipsed neural radiance fields as the leading method for photorealistic walkthroughs. The result is now in your browser, free. PlayCanvas's **SuperSplat** is an open-source editor and publisher for *3D Gaussian Splat* scenes that delivers ten-million-point walkthroughs on a mobile phone with no app to install and no subscription fee.
article.body:
The underlying science is barely three years old. In the summer of 2023, researchers at Inria and Université Côte d'Azur published a paper at SIGGRAPH showing that a scene could be represented not as a mesh or neural network but as millions of coloured, translucent ellipsoids — called **Gaussian splats** — that a GPU could rasterise at more than 100 frames per second at 1080p. The technique outperformed *NeRF* (neural radiance field), the previously dominant photorealistic reconstruction method, on both quality and speed.

PlayCanvas, a London-based WebGL engine company and subsidiary of Snap (SNAP), launched SuperSplat within months of that paper appearing. A critical clarification: SuperSplat is not a scanner. Turning photographs or video into a Gaussian splat still requires a separate tool — Polycam, Luma AI, or the open-source Nerfstudio. SuperSplat's role begins afterward: drag the exported *PLY* file into the browser, delete floating artifacts with lasso and brush selection tools, compress the scene, annotate it with guided-tour hotspots, author a camera fly-through on a timeline, and publish it to the web with a click. The resulting viewer works on mobile browsers and supports walk, fly, and orbit navigation; on compatible Android handsets it can trigger augmented-reality overlays via *WebXR*.

What sharpens the pricing contrast is that Gaussian splatting workflows have become expensive elsewhere. Polycam's cheapest tier that unlocks Gaussian Splat functionality costs $150 a year; its Business plan runs $400 per user per year. Desktop training software PostShot charges roughly €200 a year for the export tier professionals need. SuperSplat undercuts all of them at zero — MIT-licensed, with no file-size caps or export limits on any format.

The engineering answer to mobile performance is a format PlayCanvas developed called *SOGS* (Streaming Object Gaussian Splats). Rather than loading a monolithic point cloud all at once, SOGS streams a *level-of-detail* hierarchy: the viewer fetches a coarse representation first, then fills in detail as bandwidth and GPU headroom allow. PlayCanvas says SOGS handles scenes exceeding ten million Gaussians without perceptible lag on mid-range phones — a meaningful threshold for architectural scans, which routinely reach that density.

SuperSplat has accumulated more than 5,100 GitHub stars and issued 143 versioned releases since late 2023, a cadence suggesting genuine maintenance rather than a promotional launch. Whether the free-forever model survives any future shift in Snap's priorities is an open question, but the MIT licence means forks could continue independently. The dominant cost of a polished, shareable 3D walkthrough has migrated from the editing software to the capture step itself — and that is where the real frontier of democratisation remains.

concepts.definition: A scene-representation technique introduced in 2023 that encodes a 3D space as millions of tiny coloured, semi-transparent ellipsoids (Gaussians). A graphics chip can rasterise these at real-time speeds, producing photorealistic walkthroughs from a set of input photographs or video frames without a neural network.

A method for photorealistic 3D reconstruction that trains a neural network to predict the colour and density of any point in a scene from multiple input images. Dominant before 2023, but slower and more GPU-intensive at render time than 3D Gaussian Splatting.

A file format originally designed for 3D polygon meshes that has become the standard container for raw Gaussian Splat data. A PLY file for a splat scene stores the position, colour, opacity, and shape parameters of every ellipsoid in the scene.

A file format developed by PlayCanvas for SuperSplat that stores Gaussian Splat scenes in a streamable, level-of-detail hierarchy. It allows scenes with ten million or more Gaussians to load progressively on mobile devices, rather than requiring the full dataset before rendering begins.

A browser API that allows web pages to present augmented-reality or virtual-reality experiences on compatible devices — including Android phones and headsets such as the Meta Quest — without requiring a native app download.

A rendering technique that substitutes a simplified version of a scene when hardware resources are constrained, switching to more detailed geometry as those resources free up. Used in games and, now, in Gaussian Splat streaming to manage large point clouds on mobile hardware.

repos.summary: The open-source codebase for the SuperSplat 3D Gaussian Splat editor and publisher, released under the MIT licence and written primarily in TypeScript. It powers the superspl.at web app, supporting drag-and-drop editing, multi-format export (PLY, Compressed PLY, SOGS, KSPLAT, SPLAT, CSV), camera animation authoring, and one-click publishing to a hosted gallery. Over 5,100 GitHub stars and 143 versioned releases as of mid-2026 signal active, production-grade maintenance.

article.fact_check: The tweet implies SuperSplat itself creates 'a 3D scan of any building,' but it cannot capture or process photographs into a splat — that step requires a separate tool such as Polycam, Luma AI, or PostShot. SuperSplat is an editor and publisher that works on PLY files already generated elsewhere. The 'zero lag' claim is also aspirational: the SOGS streaming level-of-detail format significantly improves mobile performance, but actual smoothness varies with device GPU and scene complexity.

ticker_snap.name: Snap Inc.
ticker_snap.blurb: Snap Inc. operates Snapchat, a visual messaging app, and offers advertising products, subscription services (Snapchat+, Lens+, Snapchat Platinum), and augmented reality glasses (Spectacles). The company generates revenue primarily from advertising and faces competition from other social media platforms. As of May 2026, Snap has a market cap of about $10.3 billion and is unprofitable, with a net loss of $460 million on revenue of $5.93 billion.
ticker_snap.recent: In late April 2026, Snap announced a deal with Experian to integrate AI-powered financial education tools into Snapchat's AI Sponsored Snaps format, and disclosed an upcoming CFO transition. The stock rose 11.3% following the news, but also faced an activist investor letter pressing for a review of its Spectacles subsidiary and governance issues. As of May 6, 2026, SNAP traded at $6.11, down 9.47% after-hours.
